title: The Tour of the Fragrant Ruins
summary: A retired authority revives trade through personal influence, accompanied by a battle painter and a singer whose restrained lament contradicts the triumphal images.
source_notes: A history painter gaining patronage through a military leader becomes a tour artist whose images support political authority.
A restrained performer expressing vulnerability becomes a still singer whose lament interrupts expectations of public strength.
A retired leader reviving reforms through a regional tour becomes influence exercised outside formal office.
Long-distance spice exchange and tales concealing sources become fragrant-bark trade through human-powered maritime routes.

entries.title: Grosen of the Painted Landing
entries.body:
Grosen painted the governor above busy laborers before the harbor had fully reopened. The image attracted investment and misrepresented current capacity. He later added unfinished boats, admitting expectation without destroying the work’s role in genuine recovery.

Later accounts make Grosen of the Painted Landing the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Tour of the Fragrant Ruins. In 1206, a retired basin governor toured southern landing towns to encourage reopening fragrant-bark trade. He held no formal office but his presence changed appointments and credit. A painter accompanying him produced grand images of restored prosperity, while a nearly motionless singer performed laments for workers lost on earlier voyages. Merchants circulated fantastic stories about the bark’s remote source to protect routes and prices. The tour helped revive genuine employment but also bypassed local review of old concessions. Present households compare painted abundance, songs of vulnerability, and actual cargo accounts to decide which promises were made and which audiences merely assumed from a powerful visitor’s approval.

In the connected record, [The Fragrant Ruin Quay](b018-the-fragrant-ruin-quay.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Signature Before the Praise](b018-the-signature-before-the-praise.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether renewed trade can preserve local oversight when the commitments were encouraged by an influential person who signed no accountable undertaking.

entries.title: The Fragrant Ruin Quay
entries.body:
A ruined warehouse acquired new roof beams during the tour. Workers reused old foundations containing unresolved cargo pledges. The quay’s revival therefore increased both employment and exposure to claims that abandonment had merely postponed.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Tour Credit Circle
entries.body:
Merchants lent after interpreting the retired governor’s approval as protection. He guaranteed nothing publicly. The circle now distinguishes signed obligations from social expectation, although households already burdened by its earlier confidence cannot recover that difference cheaply.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Retired Governor’s Visit
entries.body:
Appointments changed after private meals despite the visitor holding no office. Official accounts describe spontaneous local enthusiasm. Host ledgers record which officials attended, establishing influence without pretending every decision resulted from a secret direct order.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Still Singer’s Dark Veil
entries.body:
The veil shaded a singer’s damaged eyes and became an emblem of solemn authority. Patrons copied it without the practical need. Its keeper explains the injury, preserving a person’s vulnerability within an image others prefer to treat as chosen mystique.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Lament After the Welcome
entries.body:
Hosts invite a voyage lament after praising restored commerce. Merchants call the song discouraging. Laborers say remembering losses is part of negotiating acceptable risk, making welcome and warning compatible rather than competing ceremonial moods.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Bark’s Impossible Homeland
entries.body:
A merchant tale locates fragrant trees beyond a sea of sleeping giants. Cargo evidence points to inhabited islands nearby. The story protected commercial advantage while denying actual producers visibility in the trade celebrated as a governor’s gift.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Fragrant Bark Moth
entries.body:
Moths breed beneath bark left to recover after harvest. Buyers demand complete stripping, reducing later yield. Producers preserve seasonal limits through local agreements whose practical reasoning the merchants’ fantastic origin tales make difficult to hear.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Governor’s Southern Circuit
entries.body:
The itinerary favored towns with influential hosts and bypassed struggling shallow landings. Support followed the route. Comparing included and omitted sites reveals how personal touring can direct resources without a formal allocation anyone is required to justify.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Signature Before the Praise
entries.body:
Public approval does not constitute a guarantee under this rule. Creditors must name an actual witness and undertaking. The rule protects future borrowers more readily than households whose old debts arose from confidence encouraged by the tour.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Revival’s First Short Cargo
entries.body:
A short shipment revealed overharvested bark groves and inadequate boat repairs. Lenders blamed workers’ insufficient confidence. Producer accounts showed constraints untouched by the governor’s enthusiasm, making practical revision necessary after the ceremonial opening.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Governor’s Unsigned Cup
entries.body:
A host preserved the cup used during a favorable conversation. Its authenticity proves presence, not a binding promise. Claimants still display it because the visit’s social force was real, exposing an obligation of accountability beyond what ancestor law can compel.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Source Named at Sale
entries.body:
Sellers name the producing island and harvest season before quoting a price. The custom counters fantastic source tales. Buyers sometimes prefer the mystery, forcing honest merchants to compete against a more profitable fiction.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Tour’s Missing Towns
entries.body:
A booklet records repairs requested by landings omitted from the itinerary. It includes places that declined the visit deliberately. This distinction prevents a useful pattern of unequal attention from becoming an unsupported claim that every omission was imposed.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Fragrant Warehouse Sleep
entries.body:
Workers report shared dreams of ships waiting without crews after reopening an old store. Ventilation reduced some symptoms, while dreams persisted among custodians of unfulfilled cargo pledges. Investigators separate exposure from testimony rather than treating either explanation as sufficient for all cases.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Bark Resting and Stripping
entries.body:
Gatherers alternate worked trees and preserve recovery seasons. Output cannot expand simply because markets revive. Their agreements tie delivery to inspected groves, resisting old contracts that treated future harvests as quantities assured by political favor.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Praise Without the Promise
entries.body:
Borrowers seek relief from debts encouraged by the tour. The retired governor denies a formal guarantee but offers a limited contribution. Negotiators must decide whether that contribution answers the influence he exercised or merely purchases a kinder commemorative story.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
